stem: A 42-year-old client whose parent has autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) has hypertension, flank pain, and intermittent hematuria. Imaging shows numerous cysts in bilaterally enlarged kidneys. Which condition best explains these findings?

options.B: Acquired cystic kidney disease related to advanced chronic kidney disease

rationale: NIDDK describes polycystic kidney disease as a genetic disorder in which many fluid-filled cysts grow in the kidneys and can enlarge the kidneys and reduce kidney function. ADPKD is usually diagnosed in adulthood and commonly causes pain, hypertension, and hematuria; family history is an important diagnostic clue. Therefore A best fits the complete presentation. B develops in people who already have chronic kidney disease or kidney failure, is not caused by an inherited PKD gene, and kidneys are generally normal-sized or smaller rather than enlarged from inherited cyst growth. C refers to usually harmless isolated cysts and does not explain the inherited bilateral multicystic pattern. D is a rarer recessive form whose manifestations generally begin in utero, infancy, or childhood rather than this typical adult dominant-inheritance pattern.
educational_objective: Differentiate ADPKD from acquired and simple cystic kidney disease by recognizing the adult-onset inherited pattern of numerous bilateral renal cysts, enlarged kidneys, hypertension, pain, and hematuria.
source_organization: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), NIH
source_document_title: What Is Polycystic Kidney Disease?; Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease
source_locator: What Is PKD? > definition: genetic disorder causing many fluid-filled renal cysts that can enlarge kidneys and reduce function; Types: ADPKD usually diagnosed in adulthood, ARPKD can be diagnosed in utero/soon after birth. Autosomal Dominant PKD > Signs and symptoms/complications: back or side pain, hypertension and hematuria; Diagnosis: imaging/genetic testing using age and family history. NIDDK Acquired Cystic Kidney Disease > differences from PKD: acquired disease occurs in people with CKD/kidney failure, lacks a disease-causing inherited gene, and kidneys are normal-sized or smaller rather than enlarged.
source_claim_supported: An adult with an affected parent, numerous bilateral cysts in enlarged kidneys, hypertension, pain and hematuria has the characteristic ADPKD pattern rather than acquired, simple, or recessive cystic disease.

correction_summary: Replaced the generic National Kidney Foundation citation and implausible filler alternatives with current NIH/NIDDK disease-specific sources and a clinically realistic differential among inherited, acquired, and simple cystic kidney disorders.
audit_findings: NIDDK directly supports the genetics, adult ADPKD pattern, cyst-related kidney enlargement, pain, hypertension, hematuria, and the distinction from acquired cystic kidney disease. A-D audit: A uniquely integrates adult dominant family history and enlarged multicystic kidneys; B conflicts with the inherited/enlarged-kidney pattern; C cannot explain widespread familial bilateral disease; D generally presents much earlier and has recessive inheritance. The stem supplies sufficient discriminators without requiring unsupported numeric thresholds. Blueprint is a direct NCSBN 2026 Physiological Adaptation pathophysiology match.
